Chromatin is the packaging that defines eukaryotic life, and it comes in two primary forms: euchromatin and heterochromatin. The distinction between them is both functional and historical. Scientists first told them apart cytologically by staining intensity: euchromatin stains lightly, while heterochromatin stains intensely because it is packed more tightly (Reference [1]).

Heterochromatin is the "silenced" version of the genome. It sits mostly at the periphery of the nucleus (Reference [2]). It consists mainly of genetically inactive satellite sequences, and while many genes are repressed to varying extents, some cannot be expressed even in euchromatin at all.

Heterochromatin replicates later in the S phase of the cell cycle than euchromatin does, and it is found only in eukaryotes (Reference [3]). Both centromeres and telomeres are heterochromatic, as is the Barr body of the second inactivated X chromosome in a female.

These structural details matter because they underlie gene regulation and cell division.

His characters love and desire, exult and hate, and die, with a surprising economy of vehemence and insistence.

Look at a beach and you'll often see features repeating along the shore at a regular spacing. That spacing is a longshore wavelength, and the likely cause is edge waves trapped by refraction against the shoreline. These edge waves, combined with incoming surface waves breaking on the beach, can produce longshore features with a wavelength equal to or half that of the edge wave.

Now, if a broad spectrum of edge wave modes existed, those variations would look irregular. They don't. The pattern is regular, which points to a dominant edge wave mode, and its characteristics depend on the nearshore geometry and the width of the surf zone.

Here's where you come in. Any artificial structure you build extending seawards introduces new boundary conditions, and it will almost certainly alter the edge wave spectra. You'll see this most clearly with regularly spaced structures like groynes. If you want to minimize those changes, or even put them to work, you first need to understand how edge waves behave.

Here's a fact most people miss: the Titanic was the second of three nearly identical "sister" ships built by the White Star Line. The first was the Olympic, which entered service before the Titanic on exactly the same route, with precisely the same safety features. Nobody called the Olympic unsinkable, because she never sank. The Titanic did sink, and the myth got to work, offering an explanation for the disaster. Our Classical and cultural forebears would have understood that explanation perfectly. A hundred years on, we're still fascinated by the Titanic, and that tells you something: myth, unlike the ship herself, is alive and well.

Platinum comes out of the Sudbury Basin as a by-product of nickel mining. The nickel ore is so plentiful that it makes up for platinum's scarcity: just 0.5 parts per million (ppm). The metal shows up in far higher amounts in meteorites and lunar samples. On Earth, you find it in slightly richer concentrations at impact sites, especially where volcanism followed the impact. The Sudbury Basin is the clearest example of a site where that platinum is plentiful enough to mine.
